title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
authors: Vikash Singh, Weicong Chen, Debargha Ganguly, Yanyan Zhang, Mohsen Hariri, Sreehari Sankar, Wang Yang, Chaoda Song, Alexander Nemecek, Osama Zafar, Yuting Shao, Kai Ye, Biyao Zhang, Xinpeng Li, Shouren Wang, Erman Ayday, Jing Ma, Sanmukh Rao Kuppannagari, Vipin Chaudhary
date: 10 November 2026 (arXiv v1, the only version as of 16 November 2026)

code.title: vicky157/grpo-validation
code.note: Announced in the paper as the trainer, the preregistrations and the run records. On 16 November 2026 the repository held only a README saying the code will be available soon (one commit, 11 November 2026), so nothing on this page could be checked against code or run records

takeaway: On six models of 0.6B to 4B trained with GRPO on MATH (paired seeds, mostly preregistered), a Monte-Carlo process reward that led by 1.5 points per update on Qwen2.5-1.5B (exploratory) trailed outcome-only GRPO by 14.3 points at equal generated tokens and 7.8 at equal GPU-hours (exploratory); choosing prompts with predicted success near 1/2 gained 1.7 and 0.8 points at equal tokens on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen2.5-1.5B (no significant gain on the other four models), a lead that GRPO with twice the learning rate matched on Qwen3-0.6B.
verdict: Believe the dense-reward reversal in this recipe: the deficit is large, in every seed, recurs on three Qwen3 sizes, GSM8K and longer completions, and follows from token arithmetic you can check (91% of the tokens are continuations that are never trained on). Do not stretch it to long reasoning at scale: models up to 4B, short completions, about 50 updates for the reward, one GPU type per time comparison. The prompt-selection gain is real but small and early: two of six models, about a fifth of the budget, mostly gone by twice the budget, and matched by a retuned learning rate on Qwen3-0.6B. The promised code and run records were not public on 16 November 2026.

headline.d: 50 updates against 584 in the same 12.25M tokens

headline.k: go to the reward's continuations, which are scored and discarded; per GPU-hour the gap shrinks to −7.8 points but stays in all 12 seeds
headline.d: continuations are cheap to generate, updates are not

headline.k: training on the candidates with predicted success nearest 1/2, Qwen3-0.6B (54 seeds) and Qwen2.5-1.5B (60 seeds), at equal tokens; no significant gain on the other four models
headline.d: GRPO at twice the learning rate: within 0.03 points of it on Qwen3-0.6B

resources.t: VinePPO: Refining Credit Assignment in RL Training of LLMs
resources.n: the Monte-Carlo value estimate this paper adapts (9 rollouts at every reasoning step, PPO with a KL penalty, models fine-tuned on the task); it reports reaching PPO's peak accuracy in up to 3x less wall-clock time, in a different recipe from this paper's.

resources.t: Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
resources.n: step labels from the success rate of sampled completions, the other source of the Monte-Carlo reward.

resources.t: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
resources.n: dynamic sampling, which throws away all-correct and all-wrong groups after generating them; here those discarded groups count toward the budget, and it loses 1.8 points.

resources.t: Act Only When It Pays: Efficient Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning via Selective Rollouts (GRESO)
resources.n: skips prompts whose recent groups were uniform, before generating; this paper's history filter is close to it.

kb.n: GRPO's paper, the algorithm every run here uses, and the process-supervised GRPO that collapsed here with a frozen PRM (Appendix E).

kb.t: bf16 Rounding Silently Discards Most RL Policy Updates (Fair Cast)
kb.n: the same small-Qwen GRPO setting at learning rate 10⁻⁶; this paper keeps fp32 master weights for the same reason (with pure bf16 weights, 87% of parameters did not change after one step in its check).
the Qwen3 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B models in non-thinking mode.

outcome-only RL with a rule verifier at scale; R1 lists a process reward model among its unsuccessful attempts (steps hard to judge, reward hacking, retraining cost), a different argument from this paper's cost in tokens.
